question: If learning speed itself carries an effort cost, what continuous-time learning-rate policy maximizes cumulative performance, and can a biological learner approximate the required future-performance signal?

key_findings.claim: The paper optimizes a different objective from conventional machine-learning schedulers: the time integral of task performance minus an explicit learning-effort cost, rather than final validation loss or time to a target.
key_findings.evidence: The internal reward rate is P(w(t)) minus C(mu(t)), integrated to a fixed episode horizon T with discount gamma; the default cost is beta times mu squared.

key_findings.claim: In the undiscounted continuous-time model, the optimal closed-loop rate is the square root of the expected remaining performance gain divided by the effort coefficient.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 5 gives mu-star(t) = sqrt((P(T)-P(t))/beta), derived from the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation and the terminal condition that learning effort should vanish at T.

key_findings.claim: The paper's HJB derivation does not establish Equation 5 as a globally optimal finite-horizon feedback policy because its separable value-function ansatz violates the HJB terminal boundary except along one chosen trajectory.
key_findings.evidence: The value function is defined for arbitrary starting state (t,w), which requires V(T,w)=0 for every terminal state. Section 4.1 instead assumes V(t,w)=Phi(w)+lambda(T-t) merely because the dynamics are autonomous and imposes Phi(w(T))=0 only at the realized endpoint. Applied globally, the boundary would force Phi to vanish for all w and would not solve the stated HJB. The square-root relation can still be recovered as a necessary autonomous-Hamiltonian/Euler-Lagrange conservation law along an extremal, but that is weaker than the claimed global value-function solution and does not certify a global optimum.

key_findings.claim: The apparently local controller contains a strong future oracle: P(T) is the performance reached under the optimal policy itself, at a prespecified horizon.
key_findings.evidence: The text defines P(T) under mu-star and later obtains ground-truth P(T) from a numerically optimized learning-rate episode in all simulations except MNIST; for MNIST, it searches for the P(T) value that maximizes cumulative reward.

key_findings.claim: The architecture-general derivation is conditional on autonomous deterministic gradient flow, a continuously differentiable performance, Lipschitz performance gradient, a scalar nonnegative control, and the undiscounted separable-value ansatz.
key_findings.evidence: The setup excludes ReLU-like activations, fixes every learning dynamic except scalar rate, and the exact HJB simplification sets gamma = 1 and writes V(t,w(t)) as Phi(w)+lambda(T-t).

key_findings.claim: The learn-fast-rest-later interpretation additionally assumes performance rises monotonically; it is not guaranteed by the broad smoothness conditions.
key_findings.evidence: The interpretation says P(T)-P(t) decreases because P(t) increases monotonically, while the formal setup only requires differentiability and Lipschitz gradients and the MNIST implementation uses noisy minibatches.

key_findings.claim: The closed-loop expression matches a numerically optimized schedule on one small teacher-student network and improves cumulative internal reward over tuned fixed and hand-shaped policies in the selected toy settings.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 compares the analytic controller, meta-optimization through the full training trajectory, fixed, ramp-up, and learn-then-rest profiles for a two-layer tanh network, MNIST softplus network, and one-neuron discrimination model.

key_findings.claim: The machine-learning evidence is not an independent or statistically replicated test of a general scheduler.
key_findings.evidence: For all non-MNIST analytic-controller experiments, terminal performance is copied from a numerically optimized episode; MNIST searches the P(T) value that maximizes the same cumulative reward after inserting it into Equation 5. The paper reports no seeds, error bars, test accuracy, conventional cosine/warmup/decay or adaptive-optimizer comparisons, or held-out hyperparameter protocol; the main baseline is a searched constant rate.

key_findings.claim: The episodic estimator retrieves complete final outcomes from past trajectories using similarity to the observed prefix of the current trajectory.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 21-24 whiten trajectory prefixes, weight stored episodes with a Gaussian kernel and recency decay, and predict P(T) as a weighted average of the stored episodes' final performance.

key_findings.claim: The memory result demonstrates in-distribution prefix matching, not general future-performance prediction under task or architecture shift.
key_findings.evidence: All 1,000 episodes repeatedly sample new teacher and student weights from one small two-layer generator with fixed kernel width, decay, base rate, horizon, and architecture; there is no held-out task family or learned/model-based forecaster baseline. Estimates influence the policy that generates the next prefix, while memory trajectories were generated under earlier policies, but no closed-loop distribution-shift or off-policy correction is analyzed. Whitening by a prefix standard deviation is also undefined for a constant prefix unless an unreported guard is used.

key_findings.claim: The controller can become undefined when estimated final performance falls below current performance, and no clipping or uncertainty-aware action is specified.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 5 takes a square root of P-hat(T)-P(t); the estimator reports signed errors and the discussion allows noisy or sparse P(t), but the algorithm does not state what to do for a negative estimated gap.

key_findings.claim: For isotropic Gaussian linear regression, the closed-loop condition yields an explicit tangent-shaped open-loop schedule whose remaining scalar is solved numerically.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 7-8 and the Methods derivation reduce the dynamics to a cumulative-rate ODE and give mu(t) proportional to tan of the remaining horizon, with theta fixed by a transcendental consistency equation.

key_findings.claim: The perceptron appendix contains three internally checkable equation errors, although its final Equations 7-8 and first integral are consistent with the corrected dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: From L(w)=0.5 E[(y-w^T x)^2] with x~N(0,sigma^2 I), gradient flow gives w-w* proportional to exp(-sigma^2 integral mu), not the exp(-2 sigma^2 integral mu) printed in Equation 27; Equation 28 uses the correct loss exponent and is therefore inconsistent with Equation 27. Equation 29 says to maximize positive loss plus positive effort cost, the opposite sign of the paper's reward. Differentiating the corrected negative-loss-minus-cost objective yields a coefficient sigma^4 d^2/(2 beta) in Equations 30 and 32, not sigma^2 d^2/(2 beta). Equation 33 and the main tangent solution use the corrected scaling, so these are broken intermediate derivation steps rather than a direct refutation of the final schedule.

key_findings.claim: Discounting removes the exact general solution; the paper uses a low-order homotopy-Pade approximation only for simple models and numerical meta-optimization for a two-layer network.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2.4 states that gamma below one breaks HJB tractability, presents a leading single-neuron approximation, and shows numerically that strong discounting can change a deep linear network from decay-first to delayed ramp-up.

key_findings.claim: The discounted HJB approximation is not reproducibly or quantitatively validated as an approximation theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The text states that a formal homotopy series is truncated at low order and Pade-resummed, but it does not print the chosen homotopy, mode solutions beyond the leading single-neuron expression, truncation/Pade orders, convergence conditions, or approximation error. Figure 4 only shows selected qualitative schedule shapes, and the deeper-network discounted schedules are numerical rather than analytic.

key_findings.claim: The animal comparison is qualitative and does not identify the proposed controller or its parameters.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 juxtaposes reward-rate curves from previously grouped rats with two simulated one-neuron agents; the authors explicitly state they cannot infer discount factors, effort costs, or exclude different rat strategies.

key_findings.claim: The paper explicitly disclaims the controller as a prescription for conventional deep-learning optimization.
key_findings.evidence: The limitations section contrasts cumulative performance minus learning effort with standard final-performance objectives and says the framework is a normative account for costly learning rather than ordinary scheduler design.

key_findings.claim: The experiments do not validate wall-clock, energy, instability, model-scale, or architecture-transfer claims about effort.
key_findings.evidence: Effort is the abstract beta mu-squared term; simulations use small linear or two-layer networks and downsampled MNIST, report no measured compute cost or multi-seed uncertainty, and do not test a transformer despite naming next-token prediction as an allowable performance measure.

key_findings.claim: The numerical benchmark is circular as a validation of global optimality because it differentiates through the same finite training dynamics and terminates at a locally optimal schedule.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.6 optimizes the entire schedule by gradient ascent on cumulative internal reward until convergence to a locally optimal solution; no global certificate or independent controller benchmark is supplied.

method.core_idea: Treat scalar learning speed as a costly control signal and solve for the policy that maximizes cumulative task performance net of effort over a finite learning episode.
method.mechanism: Continuous-time gradient flow supplies state dynamics. The paper inserts a separable ansatz into an undiscounted HJB equation to obtain a square-root rate based on current and optimal terminal performance; the same relation is defensible more narrowly as a necessary conservation law along an extremal. A corrected linear-regression calculation gives a tangent open-loop schedule, discounted cases use a formal homotopy-Pade approximation, and an episodic prefix-matching memory approximates the terminal-performance oracle.
assumptions: Learning follows autonomous continuous-time gradient flow, with a scalar nonnegative rate as the only control.
Performance is deterministic and continuously differentiable with a Lipschitz gradient; the text excludes ReLU-like activations from the formal model.

The advertised exact general solution uses no future discounting, an unjustified separable value-function form, a fixed horizon, and a convex effort cost with a minimum at zero; global optimality needs additional control-theoretic conditions or proof.
The learn-fast-rest-later interpretation requires current performance to increase and terminal performance to remain at least as high as current performance.
The continuous-time law ignores discrete-step stability constraints; the MNIST and memory implementations nevertheless use explicit Euler and minibatch noise.

Episodic estimation assumes relevant past trajectories and final outcomes are available, comparable after prefix whitening, and not invalidated by the controller-induced trajectory distribution shift.

techniques.role: Uses an HJB equation to optimize learning speed over a finite episode.
Computes the rate from the gap between current and expected terminal performance.
Estimates terminal performance by kernel-weighted matching to past learning trajectories.
Differentiates through full training trajectories to generate numerical reference schedules.
Derives open-loop and discounted approximations in analytically tractable gradient-flow models.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer tanh teacher-student network with four inputs, ten hidden units, six outputs, and 2,048 full-batch examples
evaluations.metric: Cumulative performance-minus-effort reward and schedule agreement
evaluations.result: The closed-loop schedule agrees with a locally meta-optimized schedule and exceeds tuned fixed and hand-shaped alternatives on the paper's objective after its terminal-performance input is taken from that optimized episode.
evaluations.baseline: Numerically optimized schedule, best flat rate, ramp-up, and learn-then-rest profiles

evaluations.setting: Two-layer softplus classifier on downsampled MNIST with minibatch SGD for 3,000 steps
evaluations.result: The noisy online controller exceeds the selected fixed baseline after tuning its terminal-performance input.

evaluations.setting: 1,000 sequential small teacher-student episodes from one task generator
evaluations.metric: Signed terminal-performance estimation error versus time, memory size, and trajectory variance
evaluations.result: Error contracts as more of the current prefix and more stored episodes become available, while high-variance trajectories remain harder.
evaluations.baseline: Uniform initial average over stored trajectories; no learned or model-based forecaster

evaluations.setting: Linear perceptron and one- or two-layer regression models
evaluations.metric: Agreement among analytic, approximate, and numerically optimized schedules
evaluations.result: The final tangent open-loop solution and leading discounted approximation track numerical solutions in selected parameter regimes, and strong discounting changes the deep-linear shape qualitatively. The printed open-loop derivation contains trajectory, sign, and coefficient errors, and the discounted approximation has no reported error bound.

evaluations.setting: Qualitative comparison with an existing rat two-alternative forced-choice experiment
evaluations.result: High- and low-learning-rate one-neuron simulations resemble slow- and fast-response rat groups, without parameter fitting or causal identification.

limitations: Author-stated: the framework is normative and not intended as a conventional deep-learning optimization prescription.
Author-stated: the biological effort cost, final-performance estimator, hard control constraints, multidimensional task allocation, and applicability beyond gradient flow are unknown or open.

Reviewer inference: the separable finite-horizon value-function ansatz does not satisfy the HJB terminal boundary for arbitrary terminal state, so the paper does not prove its global closed-loop optimality claim.
Reviewer inference: exact closed-loop control uses an optimal terminal-performance oracle and a fixed horizon; most simulations obtain that oracle from numerical optimization.
Reviewer inference: the exact derivation does not cover discounting, stochastic gradients, ReLU networks, optimizer state, weight decay, or nonstationary tasks.

Reviewer inference: the perceptron appendix contains a factor-of-two trajectory error, an objective-sign error, and a missing sigma-squared factor in two optimality equations; the final tangent form is consistent only after correcting them.
Reviewer inference: simulations are small and lack multi-seed uncertainty, measured compute or metabolic effort, conventional scheduler baselines, architecture transfer, and model or data scaling.
Reviewer inference: the discounted approximation omits its explicit homotopy, truncation/Pade orders, convergence regime, and quantitative error.
Reviewer inference: the rat comparison is descriptive and the episodic estimator is evaluated only in distribution under a controller-generated feedback loop.
failure_modes: If estimated P(T) is below current P(t), the square-root controller is undefined unless an unreported clipping or abstention rule is added.
Overestimating P(T) can cause excessive early effort or instability; underestimating it can produce premature disengagement.
A fixed episode horizon can make an otherwise useful controller brittle when training is stopped early or extended.
Episodic nearest-trajectory retrieval can fail under task, architecture, initialization, feedback-frequency, or performance-scale shift.
Prefix whitening can be undefined for zero-variance early trajectories, and no epsilon or fallback is specified.
A quadratic scalar effort proxy can recommend the wrong policy when real costs are thresholded, delayed, state-dependent, multidimensional, or coupled to wall-clock and energy.
Noisy or nonmonotone performance can make the remaining-gain signal fluctuate and invalidate the learn-fast-rest-later logic.
A continuous-time rate can be finite under the normative cost yet make an explicit Euler or minibatch implementation unstable.
Low-order homotopy-Pade approximations can leave their unreported convergence regime under strong discounting or nonlinear dynamics.
Local schedule meta-optimization can supply a self-consistent P(T) and matching curve without certifying the claimed global optimum.
reusable_insights: Learning-rate policies should declare their optimized utility: final loss, cumulative performance, wall-clock, energy, instability risk, and cognitive effort are not interchangeable.
A closed-loop formula may hide a future oracle even when it depends on only two scalar observations at execution time.
For autonomous finite-horizon control, an energy/Hamiltonian conservation identity along an extremal is not the same as a globally valid HJB feedback solution.
Dimension and sign checks on solvable special cases are high-value audits: here they expose broken intermediate equations while also showing which final formula can be salvaged.
Uncertainty over terminal performance should be part of the controller state, with abstention and safety behavior for impossible or negative gaps.
An episodic controller needs held-out task-family and architecture-shift tests, not only more episodes from one generator.
Normative optimality and mechanistic biological evidence should be reported as separate claims.
open_questions: Can a robust partially observed controller optimize cumulative performance when P(t), P(T), effort cost, and remaining horizon are uncertain?
Under what regularity, reachability, and concavity conditions is the square-root extremal globally optimal, and what is the correct finite-horizon value function?
Can the corrected perceptron derivation and the discounted homotopy-Pade approximation be released with symbolic checks, explicit orders, and uniform error bounds?
What empirical effort function best predicts human or animal learning-speed choices, and is it scalar, quadratic, and state-independent?
Does a learned terminal-performance model transfer across tasks and architectures better than episodic kernel retrieval without leaking future outcomes?
Can the HJB result be extended to discrete stochastic optimizers with momentum, adaptive preconditioning, weight decay, and nonmonotone validation performance?
How should the policy allocate effort among several simultaneous tasks under a shared control or compute budget?
Can prospective human or animal interventions distinguish terminal-performance-gap control from simpler reward-rate, difficulty, or fatigue heuristics?

competitive_landscape.title: Meta-Learning Strategies through Value Maximization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This earlier work by overlapping authors already optimizes discounted cumulative performance minus control effort using tractable average learning dynamics and studies curricula and resource allocation; the present paper's narrow addition is the scalar-rate closed form and episodic terminal-performance approximation.

competitive_landscape.title: Optimal Protocols for Continual Learning via Statistical Physics and Control Theory
competitive_landscape.difference: Mori and colleagues optimize task-selection protocols from exact low-dimensional dynamics to balance current performance and forgetting; this paper controls scalar learning speed and cumulative effort, without multi-task forgetting dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: A Statistical Physics Framework for Optimal Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Mignacco and Mori optimize curricula, dropout, and noise protocols through order-parameter dynamics for final generalization objectives; the present paper derives a simpler architecture-agnostic feedback law for a cumulative performance-minus-rate-cost objective, conditioned on terminal performance.

competitive_landscape.title: Bilevel Programming for Hyperparameter Optimization and Meta-Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Bilevel programming optimizes validation-defined outer objectives through approximate inner dynamics and provides convergence conditions for the approximation; the present work targets a cumulative normative utility and avoids full trajectory differentiation only in the undiscounted feedback derivation.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient-based Hyperparameter Optimization through Reversible Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Reversible learning differentiates exact cross-validation performance through all SGD-with-momentum steps and can optimize thousands of rate and momentum values; the present paper trades that expensive offline calculation for a two-scalar feedback rule under a narrower continuous-time objective.

competitive_landscape.title: A Nonstochastic Control Approach to Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen and Hazan cast learning rate, momentum, and preconditioner selection as online nonstochastic control and obtain regret to the best offline method across problem sequences; the present controller instead solves one finite episode with known-form gradient-flow dynamics and an effort utility.

competitive_landscape.title: AutoLRS: Automatic Learning-Rate Schedule by Bayesian Optimization on the Fly
competitive_landscape.difference: AutoLRS forecasts validation loss for candidate rates with Bayesian optimization and reports ResNet, Transformer, and BERT speedups; this paper predicts only terminal performance and applies an analytic effort controller, but lacks comparable large-network evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: AdaLRS: Loss-Guided Adaptive Learning Rate Search for Efficient Foundation Model Pretraining
competitive_landscape.difference: AdaLRS searches online using observed loss-descent velocity and reports LLM and VLM transfer across sizes and schedulers; the present paper's controller optimizes cumulative performance minus effort through an expected-terminal-performance signal and is not validated at foundation-model scale.

competitive_landscape.title: Theory of Optimal Learning Rate Schedules and Scaling Laws for a Random Feature Model
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon and Mori derive horizon-, task-spectrum-, and phase-dependent schedules for minimizing loss, jointly study batch and momentum, and test ResNet and GPT-2 regimes; this paper instead optimizes cumulative reward with an explicit effort penalty and emphasizes biological interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: What Do Near-Optimal Learning Rate Schedules Look Like?
competitive_landscape.difference: Naganuma and colleagues separate shape from base rate and search reusable finite-horizon schedules across linear regression, CIFAR-10, and WikiText-103; this paper supplies a per-trajectory feedback policy for a different cumulative-effort objective and does not search conventional schedule families.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a general closed-form, biologically plausible optimal learning-rate controller balancing effort and cumulative performance, an exact open-loop solution in simple models, discounting approximations, and episodic memory as a route to estimating future performance.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The HJB derivation, square-root feedback law, teacher-student and MNIST simulations, linear-regression solution, discounted examples, 1,000-episode memory simulation, and qualitative behavioral comparison support a coherent normative model.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Cumulative value maximization for cognitive control, meta-learning by full-trajectory differentiation, statistical-physics optimal protocols, online control, validation forecasting, and automatic foundation-model rate search are established. The credible novelty is the unusually simple square-root extremal relation for an undiscounted scalar effort objective, its explicit link to terminal-performance belief, and an illustrative episodic estimator. The paper does not prove the relation as a general globally optimal finite-horizon HJB policy: its separable value ansatz violates the terminal boundary away from one trajectory, P(T) is an endogenous oracle, and the solvable perceptron appendix contains three intermediate equation errors even though its final tangent form is salvageable. The evidence is small, unreplicated, partly oracle-tuned, and supplies neither causal biological validation nor a scalable conventional-ML scheduler result.

reviewer_notes: All 25 indexed PDF pages were reviewed, including the HJB derivation, memory estimator, perceptron calculation, discounted approximation, numerical-optimization protocol, implementation details, limitations, and eight reference-only pages. Ten exact current arXiv primary revisions were checked on 2026-08-23. The equation audit was independently recomputed from L(w)=0.5 sigma^2 ||w-w*||^2 and visually checked against PDF pages 14-15: Equation 27 has an extra factor two, Equation 29 maximizes positive loss plus cost, and Equations 30/32 omit sigma^2, while Equations 7-8 and 33 match the corrected calculation. The audit keeps the paper's normative cognitive-effort objective separate from conventional final-loss scheduling and distinguishes an extremal conservation identity from a global HJB value-function proof.
